**4. **Inflate the balloon according to device instructions and advance into the RV. RV systolic pressure rises sharply while diastolic pressure remains low.

**5. **Advance promptly into the pulmonary artery: diastolic pressure rises and a dicrotic notch appears with pulmonary valve closure.

**6. **Advance gently only until an occlusion/wedge waveform is obtained, using the minimum balloon volume. Do not repeatedly wedge or leave the balloon inflated.

**7. **Deflate the balloon and confirm return of the PA waveform, secure the catheter and interpret measurements at a consistent respiratory phase.

## 2. Waveform sequence

| Position | Typical pattern | Key point |
|---|---|---|
| RA | Low-pressure atrial a/v waves. | Confirms central/right-atrial passage. |
| RV | High systolic, very low diastolic; no dicrotic notch. | Arrhythmogenic phase — minimise dwell time. |
| PA | Similar systolic to RV but higher diastolic + dicrotic notch. | Pulmonary valve has been crossed. |
| PAOP/wedge | Atrial-like low-pressure waveform. | Only valid if truly occlusive and in an appropriate lung zone; balloon must then be deflated. |

## 3. Ventricular ectopy during insertion

Occasional ectopy is common during RV passage. If sustained ventricular ectopy or VT occurs, stop advancing and withdraw the catheter back toward the RA until the arrhythmia settles; correct hypoxaemia/electrolytes and treat haemodynamic compromise according to standard resuscitation principles. Avoid repeated traumatic passage. In a patient with pre-existing left bundle-branch block, new RBBB during passage can cause complete heart block, so pacing capability may be required.

## 4. Blood in the ETT after wedging — assume pulmonary artery injury until proven otherwise

**1. **Immediately deflate the balloon and stop further catheter manipulation/wedging.

**2. **Call for help and support oxygenation/ventilation and circulation. Reverse anticoagulation/coagulopathy where appropriate.

**3. **Position the suspected bleeding lung dependent if the side is known to protect the contralateral lung; consider lung isolation/bronchoscopy and urgent cardiothoracic/interventional support.

**4. **Do not remove the catheter blindly if it may be tamponading an injury; definitive management should be coordinated with experienced cardiac/thoracic teams.

items.title: 6. Pulse-contour monitoring and dynamic indices: when can you trust them?
items.q: A patient undergoing major surgery is monitored with an arterial pulse-contour cardiac output system displaying stroke volume, cardiac output and stroke-volume variation. Evaluate how you would use these data and the situations in which they may be misleading.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would separate three questions: is the arterial waveform technically sound, is the device’s CO/SV trend physiologically plausible, and are the assumptions required for SVV/PPV valid? I would use the monitor to guide a defined decision rather than treat every displayed number as ground truth.

## 1. What the system provides

Pulse-contour/pulse-wave systems infer stroke volume from arterial waveform morphology using proprietary models, sometimes calibrated by an independent reference method. They provide beat-to-beat SV/CO trends and often dynamic indices such as SVV or PPV. Their attraction is continuous information from an arterial catheter, but both absolute accuracy and dynamic-index validity depend on signal quality and physiology.

## 2. Before acting, validate the signal
- Check the arterial trace for damping/resonance, leveling/zeroing error and catheter problems.
- Ask whether major vasomotor change has occurred; rapidly changing vascular tone can invalidate assumptions, particularly in uncalibrated systems.
- Compare the value/trend with clinical state, NIBP, echo and response to previous interventions. A monitor that disagrees with the patient requires explanation before treatment.

## 3. SVV/PPV are conditional tests

| Condition for reliable respiratory variation | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Controlled mechanical ventilation without spontaneous effort | Irregular respiratory effort changes intrathoracic pressure unpredictably. |
| Regular rhythm | AF/ectopy causes beat-to-beat SV variation unrelated to respiration. |
| Adequate tidal excursion | Very low VT may produce too little preload variation and false negatives. |
| Closed chest / no major open thoracic effects | Open chest changes heart–lung interaction. |
| No severe RV failure/pulmonary hypertension | Respiratory variation may reflect RV afterload sensitivity rather than LV preload responsiveness. |
| Good arterial waveform | Distortion corrupts both SV calculation and dynamic indices. |

## 4. How I would use it clinically

In a suitable patient I would use SV/CO trends to test the effect of a small fluid challenge, vasopressor or inotrope. A fall in BP with preserved/high CO points away from simple hypovolaemia and toward vascular tone; a low CO with poor response to preload should prompt echo and pump/obstructive assessment rather than repeated fluid. If SVV is high under valid conditions, I still ask whether increasing flow is needed and whether fluid is tolerated.

## 5. Overall evaluation

Pulse-contour systems are useful continuous trend monitors in selected patients, but current evidence does not support assuming their absolute CO is interchangeable with thermodilution across all settings. Their clinical value depends on recognising waveform quality, calibration/device limitations and the assumptions of dynamic preload indices.

items.title: 7. Choosing haemodynamic monitoring for major surgery
items.q: A 72-year-old patient with moderate LV dysfunction is scheduled for a prolonged major abdominal operation with expected large fluid shifts. Justify your haemodynamic monitoring plan and explain how you would use it to guide fluid and vasoactive therapy.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would justify monitoring by the decisions it must support. My goals are reliable perfusion pressure, early identification of low flow or pump failure, rational testing of preload responsiveness and avoidance of both under-resuscitation and fluid overload. I would escalate from standard monitoring to an arterial line, flow monitoring and focused echo only where each adds actionable information.

## 1. Baseline and invasive pressure monitoring
- Standard PG18 monitoring plus close clinical observation and temperature/urine output as appropriate.
- Pre-induction arterial catheter is reasonable because rapid haemodynamic change, vasoactive infusion, major blood loss and frequent sampling are plausible. I would verify transducer level/zero and waveform quality before relying on it.

## 2. Flow monitoring

Because this patient has LV dysfunction and large anticipated fluid shifts, I would consider a validated SV/CO trend monitor if the team can act on it. The device might be calibrated pulse contour, oesophageal Doppler or another established platform depending on local expertise. I would not use a flow monitor simply to chase a “normal” CO; I would use it to assess response to a small preload challenge and to distinguish low flow from vasodilatory hypotension.

## 3. Focused echo as a mechanism monitor

Focused TTE/TOE becomes especially valuable if hypotension or low output is unexplained. It can identify worsening LV function, new regional dysfunction/ischaemia, RV failure, tamponade or marked underfilling. Intraoperative access may favour TOE in selected cases if TTE windows are poor and the operator is appropriately trained.

## 4. A treatment algorithm

**1. **If MAP is low, confirm the pressure and look for bleeding/anaesthetic/surgical causes.

**2. **Assess tissue perfusion and flow. If CO/SV is adequate with low SVR physiology, use vasopressor rather than repeated fluid.

**3. **If flow is low, use a valid dynamic test of preload responsiveness. Give a small bolus only if responsive, fluid is clinically indicated and there is no important congestion.

**4. **If low flow persists despite adequate preload, use echo to determine LV/RV mechanism and treat pump failure/ischaemia/arrhythmia accordingly; inotropy may be appropriate in selected low-output physiology.

**5. **Trend lactate/base deficit, urine output and capillary refill alongside haemodynamic variables. Stop interventions that fail to produce the expected physiological response.

## 5. Why I would not routinely use a PAC

Moderate LV dysfunction alone does not mandate a PAC. I would reserve it for additional complex pulmonary hypertension/RV failure, refractory mixed shock or a need for continuous pulmonary pressure/SvO₂ information that less invasive monitoring and echo cannot provide.

items.title: 8. TTE in the haemodynamically unstable anaesthetised patient
items.q: Evaluate the use of transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in a haemodynamically unstable patient under general anaesthesia.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would answer the exact question: intraoperative TTE in an unstable patient. I would evaluate its value as a rapid mechanism-finding and treatment-response tool, outline a focused scan, then balance this against intraoperative access, image quality, operator/training and time limitations. I would not turn the answer into a generic essay on TOE or preoperative echo.

## 1. Why TTE is useful in acute instability
- Rapidly differentiates major shock phenotypes: LV failure, RV failure/pressure overload, tamponade, gross underfilling/vasodilation and selected major valvular/mechanical causes.
- Can be repeated after fluid, vasopressor, inotrope, pulmonary vasodilator or decompression to determine whether the expected physiological response occurred.
- Provides anatomy and flow information that a pressure number cannot: the same MAP may occur with a small hyperdynamic LV, severe LV dysfunction or a dilated pressure-loaded RV.
- Can be integrated with lung POCUS for pulmonary oedema, pneumothorax or pleural pathology.

## 2. A focused TTE sequence

| Question | Views / findings | Management implication |
|---|---|---|
| LV? | PLAX/PSAX/apical: size and global/regional systolic function. | Low LV output → avoid blind fluid loading; address ischaemia, afterload, rhythm and consider inotropy where appropriate. |
| RV? | Apical/subcostal: RV:LV ratio, function, septal shape. | RV failure/pressure overload → support systemic pressure, reduce pulmonary vascular load, treat PE/ventilation cause, avoid RV overdistension. |
| Pericardium? | Subcostal/PLAX/apical: effusion and chamber interaction. | Tamponade physiology → urgent drainage strategy and careful preservation of venous return. |
| Forward flow / preload response? | LVOT VTI before/after PLR or small challenge. | Supports/argues against fluid only if fluid is clinically needed and tolerated. |
| Alternative major cause? | Valves/aortic root + lung POCUS adjunct. | May reveal acute MR/AR, LVOTO, pulmonary oedema or pneumothorax and redirect treatment. |

## 3. Advantages

TTE is non-invasive, available at the bedside, radiation-free and repeatable. It can provide immediate causal information during instability and can show whether treatment is working rather than relying on delayed laboratory or intermittent pressure data.

## 4. Limitations in the actual intraoperative setting
- Patient factors: obesity, hyperinflation/COPD, chest wall anatomy.
- Surgical factors: drapes, sterile field, positioning, pneumoperitoneum, open surgery and limited access to normal windows.
- Operator/training: a focused study can miss pathology and should not be over-interpreted as a comprehensive examination.
- Equipment/time: obtaining images must not delay treatment of obvious haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax or cardiac arrest.
- Intermittent rather than continuous information; TOE or invasive monitoring may be more suitable when continuous or higher-detail imaging is needed.

## 5. Translate the image into treatment

| Echo phenotype | What I would do next |
|---|---|
| Small/hyperdynamic LV + positive dynamic flow response | Look for true volume loss/vasodilation; give a small measured fluid bolus only if clinically indicated and tolerated, and use vasopressor if vascular tone remains the dominant problem. |
| Severe LV systolic dysfunction / new regional abnormality | Avoid repeated empirical fluid; support coronary perfusion, evaluate ischaemia/afterload/rhythm and consider inotropy or specialist escalation where appropriate. |
| Dilated failing RV / septal flattening | Maintain systemic pressure/RV perfusion, correct hypoxaemia/hypercapnia/acidosis, reduce pulmonary vascular load and treat the cause such as PE; avoid RV overdistension. |
| Tamponade physiology | Prioritise urgent drainage and preserve venous return/contractility until relieved. |
| No clear cardiac mechanism | Reassess haemorrhage, anaesthetic depth, tension pneumothorax, equipment and distributive causes; do not force an echo diagnosis. |

## 6. Overall evaluation

In an unstable anaesthetised patient, TTE is particularly valuable when the cause is uncertain and a rapid distinction between preload, LV, RV, obstructive and vasodilatory physiology will alter therapy. Its usefulness falls when windows/access are poor or when the operator cannot obtain/interpret a focused study reliably.

**Examiner lens:** The 2025.2 report said many candidates lost marks by giving generic uses or discussing TOE/preoperative echo. Strong answers stayed specific to intraoperative TTE, used it to distinguish shock states and assess response to therapy, and explicitly evaluated patient, surgical, training and equipment limitations.

items.title: 9. Focused echo, LVOT VTI and dynamic assessment of preload
items.q: Outline a basic focused haemodynamic TTE examination in a hypotensive patient. Explain how LVOT VTI can be used to assess changes in stroke volume and how you would avoid misusing IVC measurements.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would perform a question-driven scan rather than a full comprehensive echo: LV, RV, pericardium, forward flow and a small set of alternative diagnoses. I would use LVOT VTI primarily as a serial flow variable and treat IVC findings as contextual right-sided information rather than a standalone volume test.

## 1. Basic views and questions

| View | What I want to know |
|---|---|
| Parasternal long axis | LV size/global function, RV anteriorly, mitral/aortic valves, pericardial effusion, aortic root. |
| Parasternal short axis | Global/regional LV contraction and septal shape; D-shaped LV suggests RV loading. |
| Apical 4-chamber | RV:LV size, biventricular function, valves/pericardium. |
| Apical 5-chamber / LVOT Doppler | LVOT VTI as a forward-flow measure. |
| Subcostal 4-chamber | Pericardium/chamber interaction; often useful when other windows are difficult. |
| IVC / venous views | Right-sided pressure/congestion context only; not a definitive volume-status test. |

## 2. LVOT VTI

Stroke volume can be estimated from LVOT cross-sectional area × LVOT VTI. Because the LVOT area does not change during a short serial assessment, the percentage change in VTI can track the change in forward flow without needing a perfectly accurate absolute SV.

I would obtain the same view/sample location before and after PLR or a defined mini-fluid/fluid challenge. A meaningful rise in VTI supports preload responsiveness. In AF I would average several beats. Absolute SV is highly sensitive to LVOT diameter error because the diameter is squared when calculating area.

## 3. Why IVC alone is weak
- IVC size/collapsibility is affected by positive-pressure ventilation, PEEP, spontaneous respiratory effort, RV function, pulmonary hypertension and intra-abdominal pressure.
- A plethoric IVC may indicate high right-sided pressure/congestion, but does not tell me whether the LV will increase stroke volume with more preload.
- A small/collapsible IVC does not prove the patient needs fluid. I would combine it with dynamic flow change, ventricular function and clinical perfusion.

## 4. Link findings to treatment

The purpose of the scan is not to label chamber sizes. A small hyperdynamic LV with a positive dynamic flow response may support a carefully measured fluid trial; severe LV dysfunction argues for pump/ischaemia/afterload management; a dilated failing RV shifts priorities toward RV perfusion and reduced pulmonary vascular load; tamponade requires urgent drainage.

items.title: 10. TTE versus TOE versus PAC in complex haemodynamic instability
items.q: Compare TTE, TOE and a pulmonary artery catheter for the assessment of complex perioperative haemodynamic instability. Give examples of when you would favour each.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would compare the three by the type of information they provide, invasiveness, continuity, access and operator dependence. They are complementary rather than mutually exclusive: echo is strongest for anatomy and mechanism, while a PAC is strongest for continuous pulmonary pressure/flow/SvO₂ data in selected complex physiology.

## 1. Comparison

| Feature | TTE | TOE | PAC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main information | Ventricular/pericardial/valve anatomy + flow; lung POCUS adjunct. | High-quality cardiac/valve/aortic imaging when TTE access poor. | RA/PA pressures, PAOP, CO/CI, SvO₂ and derived SVR/PVR. |
| Invasiveness | Non-invasive. | Semi-invasive oesophageal probe. | Invasive central/right-heart catheter. |
| Continuity | Intermittent. | Can be repeated/near-continuous intraoperatively. | Continuous pressure and often CO/SvO₂ trend. |
| Major strengths | Rapid shock phenotype; treatment response; no vascular instrumentation. | Excellent intraoperative windows and structural detail. | Serial pulmonary haemodynamics and flow/oxygen-balance data. |
| Limitations | Windows/access/operator dependent. | Oesophageal contraindications/injury, training, anaesthesia dependence. | Serious complications and measurement assumptions; no routine survival benefit. |

## 2. When I would favour TTE
- Initial unexplained hypotension/shock when windows are accessible and I need a rapid mechanism diagnosis.
- Serial bedside reassessment where a non-invasive study can answer the question.
- When lung POCUS and cardiac findings together are useful.

## 3. When I would favour TOE
- Intraoperative instability with poor TTE access due to drapes/position/open surgery.
- Need for detailed valve, aortic or surgical structural assessment in an appropriately trained setting.
- Continuous/repeated cardiac imaging during major cardiac/vascular surgery.

## 4. When I would favour a PAC
- Severe pulmonary hypertension or RV failure where serial PA pressure, PVR, CO and SvO₂ directly guide therapy.
- Selected complex cardiac surgery/mechanical support or refractory mixed shock when continuous invasive data add information that echo cannot provide continuously.

## 5. Overall judgement

I would usually start with the least invasive tool that can answer the clinical question. Echo often comes early because it identifies mechanism. A PAC is justified when its unique continuous pulmonary haemodynamic/flow information is actionable and outweighs procedural risk.

items.title: 11. Applying ANZCA monitoring standards in a remote anaesthetising location
items.q: You are asked to provide general anaesthesia for an interventional radiology procedure in a remote suite. Outline how you would determine whether the location, staffing, equipment and monitoring are adequate, and what monitoring you would apply.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would start with the principle that the standard of patient safety does not fall because the procedure occurs outside theatre. I would assess the patient/procedure risk and the environment against PS55, apply PG18 clinical observation and physiological monitoring, then add case-specific monitoring and ensure rescue/recovery/transfer capability.

## 1. Decide whether this patient/procedure belongs in this location
- Patient factors: airway, comorbidity, haemodynamic/respiratory reserve, obesity/OSA, anticipated blood loss, need for advanced monitoring or postoperative support.
- Procedure factors: duration, position, limited access to the airway/patient, contrast/radiation, bleeding/vascular complications and whether the procedure itself may cause abrupt instability.
- Environment: physical space, lighting, electrical/gas supply, access to the patient, infection control, ability to evacuate/transfer and proximity of emergency support.

## 2. Staffing and rescue capability
- Appropriately trained anaesthetist and assistant; clear roles and communication with procedural staff.
- Immediate access to additional skilled help, resuscitation/defibrillation, difficult-airway equipment and emergency drugs.
- A safe recovery plan with appropriately trained staff, monitoring and transfer pathway to PACU/ICU.

## 3. Monitoring

PG18 places continuous clinical observation and vigilance alongside electronic monitoring. I would use the standard monitoring required for the anaesthetic technique — oxygenation, ventilation/capnography as appropriate, circulation with ECG/pulse and BP, inspired gases/agent where relevant — and make sure alarms are audible and enabled. BP intervals should shorten with instability; I would not accept a remote setup where the patient cannot be observed or alarms cannot be heard.

## 4. Add monitoring for specific risk

| Risk | Additional monitoring / preparation |
|---|---|
| Expected rapid BP change / vasoactive infusion | Arterial catheter; infusion pumps and secure access. |
| Major bleeding | Arterial line, serial Hb/coagulation as indicated, rapid-infusion/warming capability, blood access. |
| Severe cardiac disease | Echo/TOE or advanced haemodynamic monitoring where results will change management. |
| Long procedure / temperature risk | Temperature monitoring and active warming. |

## 5. If the suite cannot support the plan

I would change the anaesthetic technique, bring additional equipment/personnel, or move the procedure to a location that can safely support the patient. “Remote” is not a justification for lowering the standard.

items.title: 12. Choosing monitoring for a high-risk anaesthetic
items.q: A patient with severe pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction requires urgent non-cardiac surgery. Justify the monitoring you would use and explain what each addition would change in your management.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would justify each monitor against a specific threat: acute RV failure, systemic hypotension reducing RV coronary perfusion, arrhythmia, hypoxaemia/hypercapnia and abrupt changes in pulmonary vascular resistance. I would use standard monitoring plus beat-to-beat pressure, direct assessment of RV physiology and selected flow/pulmonary haemodynamic monitoring if it will change therapy.

## 1. Standard monitoring and vigilance

Apply full PG18 monitoring appropriate to GA, including continuous ECG/pulse, SpO₂, capnography/ventilation, BP and inspired gas/agent monitoring where relevant, with temperature and neuromuscular monitoring as indicated. ECG should be configured to detect rhythm/ischaemia because arrhythmia and RV perfusion failure are major hazards.

## 2. Arterial catheter

I would place an arterial line before induction if time permits. Systemic hypotension can rapidly reduce RV coronary perfusion and precipitate a spiral of RV failure; beat-to-beat pressure allows immediate vasopressor titration and repeated blood gases for oxygenation, ventilation and acid–base control.

## 3. Echo

Focused TTE or TOE, depending access and expertise, helps assess RV size/function, septal position, LV filling, pericardium and treatment response. It can distinguish low preload from RV pressure overload and guide whether fluid, vasopressor, inotrope or pulmonary vasodilator is appropriate.

## 4. PAC — selected rather than automatic

For severe pulmonary hypertension with unstable or complex physiology, a PAC may be reasonable if serial PA pressure, CO and SvO₂ will guide pulmonary vasodilator, vasopressor/inotrope and fluid decisions. I would balance this against arrhythmia/insertion risks and whether echo plus less invasive monitoring can answer the same questions.

## 5. What I am trying to prevent
- Avoid systemic hypotension, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis because each can increase RV strain or reduce RV perfusion.
- Avoid both hypovolaemia and RV overdistension.
- Detect falling CO/RV failure early and treat the cause rather than chasing a CVP target.

items.title: 13. Obtaining vascular access in the shocked patient
items.q: A shocked adult requires immediate resuscitation but has no intravenous access. Outline your approach to obtaining vascular access and justify the order of options.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

My priority is rapid delivery of the required therapy, not obtaining the most sophisticated line. I would start with the fastest high-flow peripheral option, use ultrasound early, move promptly to intraosseous access if life-saving access is delayed, and obtain central access only when its specific advantages are needed.

## 1. Immediate priorities

**1. **Call for help and define what must be delivered now: blood, fluid, vasopressor, induction drugs or all of these.

**2. **Attempt two short large-bore peripheral cannulae in accessible upper-limb sites, using ultrasound early if veins are not obvious.

**3. **If reliable access cannot be obtained rapidly in a critically unstable patient, insert an intraosseous line rather than persisting with repeated peripheral attempts.

**4. **Once initial resuscitation is underway, obtain definitive central access if needed for prolonged vasoactive infusion, poor peripheral access, specialised monitoring or device requirements.

## 2. Why short and wide matters

For laminar flow, Poiseuille’s relationship means flow rises approximately with the fourth power of radius and falls with catheter length and fluid viscosity. Therefore a short large-bore peripheral cannula is usually superior to a long narrow standard CVC lumen for rapid blood/fluid delivery.

## 3. Ultrasound and escalation
- Pre-scan the vein for patency, depth, diameter and nearby artery; visualise the needle tip and choose a catheter long enough to remain in the vessel.
- Escalate operator expertise early rather than causing multiple painful unsuccessful attempts.
- Long peripheral catheters/midlines/PICCs may suit prolonged access but are not first-choice resuscitation catheters.

## 4. Central access site choice

If central access is required, site choice depends on urgency, anatomy, compressibility/bleeding risk, pneumothorax risk, infection/thrombosis risk and operator skill. Femoral access may be rapid and compressible in shock; IJ provides excellent ultrasound anatomy; subclavian/axillary routes can be comfortable and stable but have non-compressible thoracic complications.

## 5. Reassess

Once the patient is stabilised, replace temporary/contaminated emergency access as appropriate, confirm central tip position/complications and remove devices that are no longer required.

items.title: 14. Ultrasound-guided difficult peripheral IV access
items.q: A stable but anxious patient has difficult peripheral venous access after several failed attempts. Describe how you would improve the likelihood of successful cannulation while minimising discomfort, including the role of ultrasound.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would stop repeated blind attempts, improve the conditions for cannulation, minimise pain and then use ultrasound deliberately. The procedural endpoint is not merely flashback — it is a catheter of adequate length securely positioned in a suitable vein for the intended therapy.

## 1. Reset before another attempt
- Explain the plan, acknowledge discomfort and use local anaesthetic or other analgesic measures where appropriate.
- Warm the limb, position it dependent, use gentle venous occlusion/tourniquet and optimise lighting.
- Choose an experienced operator and avoid repeatedly puncturing the same region.

## 2. Ultrasound pre-scan
- Identify a compressible non-pulsatile vein and confirm patency along its course.
- Assess depth and diameter; very deep veins need longer catheters because short cannulae dislodge after apparently successful insertion.
- Identify nearby artery/nerve and choose a trajectory that avoids them.

## 3. Needle/catheter technique

Use either short-axis/out-of-plane or long-axis/in-plane technique according to skill, but keep track of the needle tip rather than the shaft. Confirm intraluminal entry, advance the catheter rather than the needle, and visualise the catheter/wire where possible. Flush easily, check for swelling/pain and secure the catheter well.

## 4. If peripheral access is still unsuitable
- Use a longer peripheral catheter or midline for deeper veins/longer therapy.
- Choose PICC or CVC when central drug delivery or prolonged reliable access is required.
- Use IO for time-critical resuscitation rather than continuing slow elective-style attempts in an unstable patient.

items.title: 15. PICC versus percutaneous CVC for three weeks of therapy
items.q: A patient requires reliable intravenous access for three weeks of antimicrobial therapy. Compare a PICC with a percutaneous central venous catheter and outline how you would minimise the risks of PICC placement and use.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

For three weeks of therapy, I would compare the devices by insertion risk, flow, thrombosis/infection, patient comfort and intended use. A PICC is attractive for prolonged stable therapy but is not automatically safer overall, particularly because thrombosis and occlusion matter. I would then outline risk reduction from device selection through insertion, tip confirmation, maintenance and timely removal.

## 1. Comparison

| Issue | PICC | Percutaneous CVC |
|---|---|---|
| Insertion | Arm insertion avoids insertion-related pneumothorax and major neck/chest arterial injury. | IJ/subclavian/femoral insertion has site-specific mechanical risks. |
| Duration / outpatient care | Well suited to weeks–months and often convenient for mobilisation/outpatient therapy. | Suitable for acute/short-medium term; neck/groin access can be less convenient. |
| Flow | Long/narrow — poor for rapid high-flow resuscitation. | Can provide larger/shorter lumens or introducer access for high-flow therapy. |
| Thrombosis | Upper-extremity thrombosis is an important risk, especially larger/multilumen devices. | Thrombosis risk remains but differs by site/device. |
| Infection | CLABSI risk still requires bundle care. | CLABSI risk also important; site and maintenance matter. |
| Mechanical issues | Malposition, occlusion, migration; no thoracic insertion complication. | Pneumothorax/haemothorax, arterial injury, malposition, bleeding. |

## 2. Minimise PICC risk before insertion
- Confirm that central access is actually required and choose the minimum number of lumens/diameter needed.
- Assess upper-limb veins with ultrasound for patency, size and thrombosis risk; avoid unnecessarily small veins/large catheters.
- Use an appropriate vein/site and full aseptic technique.

## 3. Safe insertion and confirmation

**1. **Use real-time ultrasound-guided venepuncture and a controlled wire/catheter technique.

**2. **Advance to an appropriate central tip position.

**3. **Confirm tip location using the local validated method before using the line for therapies that require central placement.

**4. **Secure and dress the line to reduce migration and contamination.

## 4. Maintenance and removal
- Use an evidence-based central-line infection-prevention bundle and aseptic access technique.
- Monitor for arm swelling/pain, catheter dysfunction, infection and thrombosis.
- Remove the catheter as soon as the indication ends; unnecessary catheter-days create avoidable infection/thrombosis risk.

**Examiner lens:** The historical PICC SAQ expected a balanced comparison rather than “PICC is safer”: lower pneumothorax/major arterial injury risk was offset by thrombosis concerns, and risk reduction needed to include placement confirmation, line-care bundle principles, minimum lumens and removal when no longer required.

items.title: 16. Central venous catheter site selection and safe insertion
items.q: You decide that a central venous catheter is required. Compare internal jugular, subclavian/axillary and femoral routes, then describe a safe ultrasound-guided Seldinger insertion and the important complications.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would first justify the site as a trade-off between urgency, anatomy, compressibility, pneumothorax risk, infection/thrombosis, patient mobility and future access. I would then describe a real-time ultrasound-guided Seldinger technique with explicit wire control and confirmation, followed by immediate and delayed complications.

## 1. Site comparison

| Site | Advantages | Important disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| Internal jugular | Excellent ultrasound visualisation; compressible; familiar; easy tip path. | Carotid/neck haematoma risk; infection/thrombosis; uncomfortable; neck movement affects dressing. |
| Subclavian/axillary | Comfortable/stable dressing; lower infection risk in some data. | Pneumothorax/haemothorax; non-compressible arterial injury; stenosis; preserve subclavian veins in future dialysis patients. |
| Femoral | Fast, compressible, no pneumothorax; useful during CPR/neck/chest constraints. | Groin contamination, thrombosis, mobility/dressing problems. |

## 2. Safe Seldinger sequence

**1. **Confirm indication, consent/urgency, coagulation context, site and rescue plan; monitor and position the patient.

**2. **Use full aseptic precautions and a covered ultrasound probe. Pre-scan the vein/artery, patency, depth and adjacent structures.

**3. **Puncture the vein under real-time ultrasound while visualising the needle tip.

**4. **Confirm venous access before dilation; visualise the guidewire within the target vein and use additional confirmation if uncertainty exists.

**5. **Maintain continuous control of the wire. Never release it and never force resistance.

**6. **Dilate only after confirming wire position, advance the catheter, remove the wire, aspirate/flush all lumens, secure and dress.

**7. **Confirm tip position and exclude complications using the site/device/local validated method before high-risk use.

## 3. Complications

| Immediate/mechanical | Delayed |
|---|---|
| Arterial puncture/cannulation, bleeding/haematoma, pneumothorax/haemothorax, air embolism, arrhythmia, guidewire loss/knotting, malposition, perforation/tamponade, nerve injury. | CLABSI, thrombosis, stenosis, occlusion, migration, catheter fracture/device failure. |

## 4. Practical prevention
- Ultrasound reduces mechanical complications but does not replace sterile technique or wire discipline.
- Use the minimum necessary lumens and remove the line promptly when no longer required.
- If an arterial dilator/large catheter has been placed inadvertently, do not simply pull it out — obtain urgent vascular/specialist advice for controlled removal/repair.

items.title: 17. Maximising rapid intravenous fluid/blood delivery and using rapid infusers safely
items.q: Describe the factors that determine the maximum achievable rate of intravenous fluid administration. Outline the issues and hazards associated with rapid infusion devices.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would answer this from fluid mechanics and the complete delivery system: driving pressure, catheter radius/length, fluid viscosity and every resistance in the circuit. I would then discuss rapid-infuser benefits, device/circuit hazards and the physiological consequences of delivering large volumes of cold blood or fluid quickly.

## 1. Determinants of flow

| Factor | Effect on flow / practical meaning |
|---|---|
| Radius / internal diameter | Dominant effect: for laminar flow, flow is proportional to radius⁴. A short large-bore cannula dramatically outperforms a narrow catheter. |
| Length | Flow is inversely proportional to length; long PICCs and standard CVC lumens are poor for rapid resuscitation. |
| Driving pressure | Pressure bags/pumps/rapid infusers increase flow if the circuit can tolerate it. |
| Viscosity | Blood flows more slowly than crystalloid; warming reduces viscosity somewhat and prevents hypothermia. |
| Circuit resistance | Filters, narrow connectors, stopcocks, extension tubing and partially kinked lines reduce flow. |
| Catheter position / vein | Catheter against wall, thrombosis, small vein or extravasation limits effective delivery. |

## 2. Practical setup in major haemorrhage
- Use short large-bore peripheral access or an appropriately large central introducer rather than a long narrow lumen.
- Minimise unnecessary connectors/long extension sets; use compatible blood filters and warming/rapid-infusion circuits.
- Secure lines and check the full circuit before applying high pressure.

## 3. Rapid-infusion device hazards
- Air entrainment/air embolism if the reservoir or tubing is allowed to run dry or air-detection safeguards are bypassed.
- Line/catheter disconnection or rupture with sudden blood/fluid loss into the environment or tissue extravasation.
- Haemolysis risk depends on device, pressure, catheter and product; avoid inappropriate narrow high-resistance circuits.
- Very rapid transfusion increases citrate load/hypocalcaemia, potassium delivery and volume shifts; monitor ionised calcium/electrolytes in major haemorrhage.
- Inadequate warming causes hypothermia and worsens coagulopathy; device warming has temperature/flow limits.
- The rapidity of delivery can outpace clinical reassessment and cause overload if the haemorrhage has been controlled.

## 4. Overall safety principle

A rapid infuser is a delivery tool, not a resuscitation strategy. It should sit within a major-haemorrhage plan with source control, blood-component strategy, warming, calcium/electrolyte monitoring and clear communication about cumulative volume.

items.title: 18. Invasive versus non-invasive blood pressure monitoring in morbid obesity
items.q: Evaluate invasive and non-invasive blood pressure monitoring options in a patient with morbid obesity undergoing major surgery.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would evaluate both techniques specifically in obesity, not give generic pros and cons. I would discuss cuff fit/arm geometry and intermittent measurement limitations, then weigh the accuracy and beat-to-beat advantages of an arterial line against technical difficulty and invasive complications.

## 1. Non-invasive BP: advantages in this patient
- Non-invasive and avoids arterial cannulation complications.
- Easy to repeat at different sites/cuff sizes and adequate for many stable patients if a validated, properly fitting cuff is available.
- Useful as an independent comparison even when an arterial line is present.

## 2. Non-invasive BP: obesity-specific limitations
- Large or conical upper arms may make standard cuff fit poor; a cuff that is too small can over-read and an unsuitable cuff can give erratic values.
- Forearm/wrist alternatives may not be interchangeable with upper-arm reference values and should be interpreted cautiously.
- Movement, arrhythmia, severe vasoconstriction and low perfusion worsen oscillometric reliability.
- Intermittent cycling may miss abrupt changes during induction, positioning, pneumoperitoneum or bleeding.

## 3. Invasive arterial BP: advantages
- Beat-to-beat pressure during induction and major surgery; immediate feedback when vasoactive drugs are titrated.
- Frequent arterial sampling for gas, haemoglobin and metabolic assessment.
- Avoids repeated dependence on difficult cuff fit once a reliable arterial system is established.

## 4. Invasive arterial BP: obesity-specific disadvantages and general risks
- Arterial palpation/anatomy and securement may be more difficult; ultrasound can improve success.
- Invasive complications: bleeding/haematoma, infection, thrombosis/ischaemia, pseudoaneurysm, nerve injury and accidental intra-arterial injection.
- The transducer system itself can be wrong: damping, leveling or zeroing errors can produce precise-looking but misleading numbers.

## 5. My choice

For major surgery with anticipated rapid haemodynamic change or vasoactive therapy, I would favour an arterial catheter while retaining an appropriately sized NIBP cuff for cross-checking. For minor stable surgery, a validated correctly sized NIBP setup may be entirely adequate. The decision is driven by procedural/patient risk, not BMI alone.

**Examiner lens:** The 2025.1 report specifically criticised answers that gave generic invasive/NIBP pros and cons without applying them to morbid obesity. The command word was “evaluate”, so both advantages and disadvantages of each method had to be weighed in the obese patient.

items.title: 19. Damped arterial waveform: troubleshooting, damping and leveling
items.q: After radial arterial cannulation, the waveform appears damped and the pressure is 78/52 mmHg while the cuff reads 108/64 mmHg. Describe your assessment of the discrepancy and how you would ensure the arterial line is accurate.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would not immediately treat the arterial-line number. I would first assess the patient and compare independent signals, then troubleshoot the catheter and fluid-filled system, re-level/zero, use a square-wave test to identify damping, and only then decide which pressure is clinically credible.

## 1. Look at the patient and independent measurements
- Check pulse/perfusion, surgical context, ECG and whether there is a genuine low-output state.
- Repeat NIBP with an appropriate cuff and compare another pulse waveform/plethysmograph.
- A small arterial waveform may be genuine in profound low output/vasoconstriction, but a large unexplained discrepancy raises suspicion of measurement error.

## 2. Check the arterial catheter
- Inspect wrist/limb position, catheter kink, partial withdrawal, vasospasm, clot or catheter tip against the vessel wall.
- Check distal perfusion and the insertion site for bleeding/haematoma.

## 3. Check the tubing/transducer system
- Air bubbles, clot, long/compliant tubing, multiple stopcocks and loose connections commonly overdamp the trace.
- Make sure the flush bag is pressurised and the line is patent; remove bubbles/clot and unnecessary compliance/resistance.
- Re-level the transducer to the intended anatomical reference and re-zero to atmosphere if required.

## 4. Damping and the square-wave test

| Pattern | Effect | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Overdamped | Slurred upstroke, low systolic/high diastolic, narrow pulse pressure; MAP often less affected. | Air/clot/compliant tubing/kink/partial occlusion. |
| Underdamped / resonant | Systolic overshoot, low diastolic, ringing; MAP often less affected. | Stiff/high-frequency system, catheter whip/resonance. |

Briefly activate the fast flush to generate a square wave. Excess oscillations after release suggest underdamping; a sluggish return with minimal oscillation suggests overdamping. The test assesses the monitoring system, not the patient.

## 5. Leveling in unusual positions

Hydrostatic pressure changes by about 0.74 mmHg per centimetre vertical height. A transducer below the reference level reads falsely high and above it falsely low. In beach-chair/sitting surgery, if cerebral perfusion is the target, I must account for the vertical distance between the heart and brain rather than assuming a heart-level MAP represents cerebral arterial pressure.

## 6. Final action

Until the system is corrected, I would use the pressure that best fits the patient and independent measurements, with particular attention to MAP. I would not titrate potent vasopressors to an obviously unreliable trace.

items.title: 20. Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy for major surgery
items.q: Discuss the principles and role of goal-directed haemodynamic therapy (GDT) for a high-risk patient undergoing major surgery. Describe a practical algorithm and the limitations of the approach.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would define modern GDT as iterative treatment of inadequate perfusion using pressure, flow and dynamic preload assessment — not a fixed fluid recipe or a drive to maximise cardiac output in everyone. I would describe who may benefit, a stepwise fluid/vasopressor/inotrope algorithm and the limitations of monitor- and protocol-dependent evidence.

## 1. Who may benefit
- High-risk patients having major surgery with expected haemodynamic instability or large fluid shifts.
- Patients in whom both under-resuscitation and fluid overload have important consequences.
- Settings with a trained team, a reliable monitor and a protocol that links measurements to treatment.

## 2. Define the physiological goals

The goals are adequate organ perfusion and oxygen delivery, not a normal CVP or a maximised SV. I would assess MAP/pressure, SV/CO/flow, haemoglobin and saturation, and tissue-perfusion indicators such as capillary refill, lactate trajectory, urine output and clinical organ function.

## 3. Practical algorithm

**1. **Identify inadequate perfusion or a high-risk haemodynamic problem.

**2. **If pressure is low, assess mechanism. Treat important vasodilation with vasopressor once preload has been reasonably addressed.

**3. **If flow is low, test fluid responsiveness dynamically rather than using static pressure.

**4. **If responsive, ask whether fluid is actually indicated and tolerated. Give a small defined bolus only when the answer is yes.

**5. **If low flow persists despite adequate preload, use echo to identify LV/RV dysfunction or obstruction and use cause-specific therapy/inotropy where appropriate.

**6. **Reassess the same flow/perfusion endpoints and stop ineffective or harmful therapy.

## 4. What GDT should not become
- Repeated fluid until SV can no longer be increased, regardless of congestion.
- Fixed CVP or ScvO₂ targets derived from historical early-goal-directed-therapy protocols.
- A reason to insert advanced monitors in low-risk patients where the data are unlikely to change management.
- Treatment of a monitor number without assessing the patient and the haemodynamic mechanism.

## 5. Evidence and limitations

The effect of perioperative GDT varies with patient selection, protocol and implementation. Benefits are more consistently seen in selected reductions in complications or length of stay than as a universal mortality effect. Monitor error, invalid dynamic indices and protocol non-adherence can all make GDT ineffective or harmful. Contemporary perioperative guidance therefore emphasises individualised targets rather than routine maximisation of SV/CO.

items.title: 21. Interpreting lactate, base deficit, SvO₂/ScvO₂ and capillary refill
items.q: Outline how you would use lactate, base deficit, mixed/central venous oxygen saturation and bedside perfusion markers to assess and guide resuscitation in shock. Include important limitations of each.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would use these variables as complementary trends, not interchangeable targets. I would explain what each reflects, major confounders, and how an abnormal result changes my next question about pressure, flow, oxygen content or metabolic demand.

## 1. Lactate

Lactate is a useful severity and trajectory marker, but not a synonym for tissue hypoxia or hypovolaemia. It may rise from adrenergic stimulation, seizures, impaired hepatic clearance, drugs/metabolic effects and regional/global hypoperfusion. A falling lactate after treatment is reassuring when the cause is perfusion-related, but the expected rate of clearance depends on production and clearance.

## 2. Base deficit

Base deficit reflects the metabolic component of acid–base disturbance and can track shock burden, particularly in haemorrhagic/trauma contexts. It is not specific: saline-related hyperchloraemia, renal failure, ketoacidosis and other metabolic processes alter it. I would interpret it with pH, chloride, lactate and the clinical picture.

## 3. SvO₂ and ScvO₂

| Finding | Possible interpretation |
|---|---|
| Low SvO₂/ScvO₂ | Low CO, anaemia, hypoxaemia or increased oxygen consumption from fever/shivering/pain/work of breathing. |
| Normal/high despite shock | Distributive shunting or impaired extraction; low metabolic demand, deep sedation or hypothermia; does not exclude regional hypoperfusion. |

SvO₂ is true mixed venous blood from the pulmonary artery; ScvO₂ from the SVC is easier to obtain but is not numerically interchangeable in all shock states. I would never respond to a low value with fluid automatically — I would inspect CO, Hb, SaO₂ and metabolic demand.

## 4. Capillary refill, skin temperature and mottling

These bedside markers are rapid and repeatable. Prolonged capillary refill, cool peripheries and mottling support poor peripheral perfusion, while improvement after treatment may be clinically meaningful. Ambient temperature, vasopressors and peripheral vascular disease confound them, so they should complement haemodynamic and metabolic data.

## 5. Integrate rather than chase targets

A patient with MAP 70, high lactate, prolonged capillary refill and low CO requires a different response from a patient with the same lactate but high CO and warm distributive physiology. My goal is to use the markers to identify which component of oxygen delivery/perfusion remains inadequate and then treat that mechanism.

items.title: 22. Goal-directed resuscitation in sepsis: what changed from early GDT?
items.q: Discuss a contemporary goal-directed haemodynamic approach to septic shock and explain how it differs from historical early goal-directed therapy based on fixed CVP and ScvO₂ targets.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would acknowledge that early goal-directed therapy was historically important but that modern sepsis resuscitation has moved away from fixed CVP/ScvO₂ protocols. Contemporary care is individualised: early infection/source treatment, appropriate initial fluid, vasopressors for vasodilatory hypotension, dynamic testing before ongoing fluid, early echo in unresolved shock and serial assessment of perfusion.

## 1. Immediate sepsis priorities
- Recognise shock, obtain appropriate cultures without delaying therapy, give timely antimicrobials and pursue source control.
- Assess perfusion and haemodynamic phenotype while initial resuscitation begins.
- Correct major hypoxaemia, severe anaemia/bleeding or other contributors to oxygen delivery when present.

## 2. Fluids — initial treatment, then stop guessing

Initial crystalloid may be appropriate when there is likely intravascular deficit and tissue hypoperfusion, but persistent hypotension after initial treatment should trigger reassessment rather than repeated litres. Current haemodynamic guidance favours dynamic assessment of fluid responsiveness before further fluid and attention to fluid tolerance/congestion.

## 3. Vasopressors and flow

Vasodilatory hypotension requires vasopressor support once preload is reasonably addressed; waiting for an arbitrary fluid volume before starting vasopressors can be harmful. If shock persists, measure/estimate CO and use echocardiography to define LV/RV function. Selected low-output septic cardiomyopathy may need inotropy, while RV failure requires a different strategy.

## 4. Perfusion endpoints
- Serial capillary refill and clinical perfusion.
- Lactate trajectory interpreted in context, not “normalise lactate with fluid”.
- Urine output/organ function and haemodynamic response.
- SvO₂/ScvO₂ only when available and interpreted as an oxygen-delivery/consumption balance rather than a fixed universal target.

## 5. Difference from historical EGDT

Historical EGDT used protocolised CVP and ScvO₂ thresholds. Modern practice recognises that static CVP is poor for predicting fluid responsiveness and that a normal/high venous saturation can coexist with distributive shock. The contemporary “goal” is individualised restoration of perfusion using dynamic physiology, not attainment of fixed invasive numbers.

items.title: 23. Perioperative fluid prescription for a low-risk adult
items.q: A healthy 70 kg adult is fasting for an uncomplicated two-hour elective operation with minimal expected blood loss and early postoperative oral intake. Describe and justify your perioperative intravenous fluid plan.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would first decide whether IV fluid is required at all, then separate maintenance from resuscitation and replacement. In this low-risk patient I would avoid routine replacement of a large “fasting deficit” or theoretical third-space loss, use a balanced isotonic crystalloid only for actual need, and aim for early return to oral intake.

## 1. Preoperative considerations

With modern fasting practice, many patients can have clear fluids until relatively close to surgery according to local policy, so the historical calculation of a large fasting deficit is usually inappropriate. I would assess actual intake, vomiting/diarrhoea, diuretics, renal/cardiac disease and clinical signs of dehydration rather than assume hypovolaemia from fasting alone.

## 2. Intraoperative plan
- If IV fluid is needed, a balanced isotonic crystalloid is a reasonable default.
- For a short low-risk case with minimal losses, use a modest rate sufficient for actual maintenance/therapy rather than a fixed large-volume formula.
- Replace measured blood or other losses according to their nature. Significant blood loss becomes a blood-management problem, not simply more crystalloid.
- If hypotension occurs, identify vasodilation, low preload, pump failure, arrhythmia or obstruction before giving repeated fluid.

## 3. Maintenance framework if oral intake is delayed

A common adult starting point is roughly 25–30 mL/kg/day of water with approximately 1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium, potassium and chloride and limited glucose to reduce starvation ketosis, adjusted for age, renal/cardiac function, other intake and laboratory values. For this 70 kg adult that is a daily framework, not a reason to infuse the entire requirement during the two-hour operation.

## 4. Postoperative plan

Encourage oral intake when safe and stop IV maintenance once it is no longer needed. Reassess fluid balance, urine output, electrolytes and symptoms rather than continuing fluid by inertia.

items.title: 24. Choosing the intravenous fluid and knowing when to stop
items.q: Compare balanced crystalloid, 0.9% saline, glucose-containing fluid, albumin and blood components for perioperative use. Give examples of appropriate indications and important limitations, and describe how you would reassess ongoing fluid therapy.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would choose fluid by indication and composition, not by habit. I would distinguish maintenance, resuscitation, replacement and haemorrhage, then prescribe a dose/rate with a clinical endpoint and stop rule.

## 1. Fluid choice

| Fluid | Useful indication | Important limitations |
|---|---|---|
| Balanced isotonic crystalloid | Default resuscitation/replacement for many perioperative patients. | Large volumes still cause oedema/dilution; electrolyte composition must fit the patient. |
| 0.9% saline | Specific sodium/chloride needs and selected neuro/metabolic contexts. | Large volumes cause high chloride load and hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis; may be undesirable in susceptible patients. |
| Glucose-containing fluid | Hypoglycaemia prevention/treatment and selected maintenance/paediatric/metabolic needs. | Not a resuscitation fluid after glucose is metabolised; dysglycaemia and hyponatraemia risk depend on formulation/volume. |
| Albumin | Selected critical-care/perioperative situations where colloid is specifically justified. | Cost; not routinely required; does not replace RBCs or haemostatic components. |
| Blood components | Haemorrhage with loss of oxygen-carrying capacity and/or haemostatic components. | Requires transfusion/haemostasis strategy and complication monitoring; not simply “volume replacement”. |

## 2. Reassessment
- Haemodynamics and perfusion: BP, capillary refill, SV/CO response where monitored.
- Fluid tolerance/congestion: lungs, oxygenation, CVP/venous congestion in context, peripheral oedema and RV function.
- Renal/electrolyte status: urine output, creatinine, sodium/chloride/potassium and acid–base status.
- Cumulative balance and weight, recognising charted balance may be inaccurate.

## 3. Stop rules

Stop a resuscitation bolus when the expected haemodynamic response is absent or harm appears. Stop maintenance IV fluid when oral/enteral intake is adequate. After the shock/resuscitation phase, patients with accumulated excess fluid may need active de-resuscitation once perfusion is stable.

## 4. One-sentence exam rule

For every IV fluid prescription state: indication → fluid/composition → dose/rate → endpoint → reassessment/stop rule.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
Examiners expect you to name the trial, say what it tested, give the headline result and say why it changed practice. Links open the paper on PubMed (or the open-access copy).

## Cardiac output monitoring and filling pressures

| Trial | Design | Headline result | Why it matters | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Marik et al., Chest 2008 | Systematic review: CVP versus blood volume and fluid response | Pooled correlation of CVP with blood volume 0.16; CVP did not predict response to a fluid challenge | Foundation of the "CVP cannot guide fluids" argument | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18628220/) |
| Marik and Cavallazzi, Crit Care Med 2013 | Updated meta-analysis (43 studies) | AUC 0.56 (95% CI 0.54–0.58); correlation 0.18; same in ICU and operating room; 57% responders | CVP is not a basis for fluid decisions | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23774337/) |
| Marik et al., Crit Care Med 2009 | Systematic review of dynamic arterial waveform indices | AUC 0.94 PPV, 0.84 SVV, 0.86 SPV versus 0.55 CVP; valid only with controlled ventilation | Why dynamic indices replaced static pressures | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19602972/) |
| SUPPORT (Connors, JAMA 1996) | Observational cohort, 5735 ICU patients | PAC associated with higher 30-day mortality (OR about 1.24) | Triggered the PAC trials; association, not proof of harm | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8782638/) |
| Sandham, NEJM 2003 | RCT of PAC-guided GDT in elderly high-risk surgical patients | No mortality benefit; more pulmonary emboli in the PAC group | PAC not routinely useful in high-risk surgery | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12510037/) |
| PAC-Man (Harvey, Lancet 2005) | Pragmatic RCT, 65 UK ICUs, over 1000 patients | Hospital mortality 68% versus 66%; adjusted HR 1.09 (0.94–1.27) | No clear benefit or harm; PAC not an intervention itself | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16084255/) |
| ESCAPE (JAMA 2005) | RCT in advanced heart failure | No difference in days alive and out of hospital | PAC-guided therapy safe but not superior to clinical assessment | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16204662/) |
| FACTT (NEJM 2006) | RCT in acute lung injury: PAC versus CVC, and fluid strategy | No benefit of PAC; conservative fluid strategy improved ventilator-free days | Fluid strategy mattered more than the monitor | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16714768/) |
| Rajaram, Cochrane 2013 | Meta-analysis of 13 trials, 5686 patients | No difference in mortality, ICU stay or cost | Confirms neutrality of PAC in ICU and high-risk surgery | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23450539/) |

## Goal-directed therapy and perioperative fluids

| Trial | Design | Headline result | Why it matters | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| OPTIMISE (Pearse, JAMA 2014) | RCT, 734 patients, major GI surgery, cardiac output-guided algorithm | Primary composite not significantly reduced; meta-analysis suggested fewer complications | Equivocal evidence for flow-guided therapy | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24842135/) |
| OPTIMISE II (BMJ 2025) | RCT, 2498 patients aged 65 or older, major elective GI surgery | Postoperative infection 23.2% versus 22.7%; more early cardiac events with the intervention | Contemporary trial: cardiac output-guided fluid and low-dose inotrope did not help | [BMJ 2025 (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12036648) |
| RELIEF (Myles, NEJM 2018) | RCT, 3000 patients, major abdominal surgery, restrictive versus liberal fluids | Disability-free survival at 1 year 81.9% versus 82.3% (HR 1.05); AKI 8.6% versus 5.0% | Restriction is not better and increases AKI; ANZCA and ANZICS-led trial | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29742967/) |
| SAFE (NEJM 2004) | RCT, ICU, albumin versus saline | No overall difference; harm in traumatic brain injury subgroup | Albumin is safe overall; avoid in TBI | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15163774/) |
| SPLIT (JAMA 2015), SMART (NEJM 2018), PLUS (NEJM 2022) | Balanced crystalloid versus saline in critically ill patients | Little or no difference in mortality; SMART showed fewer major adverse kidney events | Balanced crystalloids are a reasonable default | [SPLIT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26444692/) · [SMART](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29768150/) · [PLUS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35041780/) |
| 6S and CHEST | Hydroxyethyl starch versus crystalloid in ICU | More renal replacement therapy with starch | Starches should not be used in the critically ill | [6S](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22738085/) · [CHEST](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23075127/) |

## Shock, sepsis and perfusion targets

| Trial | Design | Headline result | Why it matters | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rivers, NEJM 2001 | Single-centre RCT of early goal-directed therapy (CVP, MAP, ScvO₂ targets) | Large mortality reduction (30.5% versus 46.5%) | Launched EGDT; not reproduced | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11794169/) |
| ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe | Three multicentre RCTs of EGDT versus usual care (ARISE was Australasian) | No mortality benefit in any trial | Protocolised EGDT abandoned | [ProCESS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24635773/) · [ARISE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25272316/) · [ProMISe](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25776532/) |
| PRISM (NEJM 2017) | Individual patient data meta-analysis of the three trials, 3723 patients | 90-day mortality 24.9% versus 25.4%; adjusted OR 0.97 (0.82–1.14); higher costs with EGDT | Definitive: no subgroup benefits | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28320242/) |
| CLASSIC (2022), CLOVERS (2023) | RCTs of restrictive versus standard or liberal fluids in septic shock | No difference in 90-day mortality | Fluid volume matters less than the early basics | [CLASSIC](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35709019/) · [CLOVERS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36688507/) |
| ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (JAMA 2019) | RCT: capillary refill-targeted versus lactate-targeted resuscitation | Trend to lower mortality with capillary refill targeting, not statistically significant | Peripheral perfusion is a legitimate target | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30772908/) |

## Vascular access

| Trial | Design | Headline result | Why it matters | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chopra, Lancet 2013 | Meta-analysis of PICC and venous thromboembolism | PICCs carried a higher risk of DVT than other central lines in hospitalised patients (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.54 to 4.23, in 11 comparative studies; number needed to harm about 26) | PICC is not automatically the safer central line | [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23697825/) |
| Brass, Cochrane 2015 | Meta-analysis of ultrasound for central venous cannulation | Ultrasound guidance reduces failure and complications, most clearly for the IJ | Basis for ultrasound as standard of care | [IJ](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25575244/) · [Subclavian/femoral](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25575245/) |

**Exam technique for trials:** give the name and year, the population, the intervention and comparator, the primary outcome and result, and one sentence on the implication or limitation (for example single-centre, usual care changed, surrogate endpoint). Do not quote figures you are not sure of; a correct qualitative statement scores better than a confident wrong number.
